LESSON 96 OF 106·Defensive Operations: Detect, Respond, Recover

Business Continuity, Disaster Recovery and Resilience

The plans that exist for the day the systems do not: what continuity and recovery each promise, how the objectives are set, and why an untested plan is not a plan.

Applied Foundation15 min
Why this matters

Security and availability are usually in tension, and resilience is the discipline that resolves it. The question is not whether you can prevent everything, but whether you can keep operating while you deal with what you cannot prevent.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Business impact analysis establishes which services matter most and what their tolerable downtime is.
  • Recovery time and recovery point are different questions, and a plan has to answer both for each service.
  • Resilience means surviving degradation, not only avoiding failure, so a reduced mode of operation should exist.
  • Plans fail because of assumptions about systems and people that are no longer true.
  • Exercises test the plan, and an untested plan is a document with good intentions.

The background

  • Continuity planning started as disaster recovery for datacentres, focused on restoring hardware.
  • It broadened to include processes and people, which is where most real disruption actually lands.
  • Cloud services changed the recovery options without changing the underlying questions.
  • Resilience became a board-level concern as dependence on digital services increased.

Real-world examples

  • A business that can operate manually for two days has far more options than one that cannot.
  • A ransomware event where staff cannot be paid or customers cannot be reached becomes a business problem, not a technical one.
  • A plan that lists a recovery time no supplier has ever committed to is fiction.

What to look for

  • Check whether the plan names recovery times per service and whether they were agreed with the business, not only with IT.
  • Check whether a reduced manual mode is defined and has been practised.
  • Check what the plan assumes about staff availability, since that assumption breaks during an incident.
  • Check when the plan was last exercised and what the exercise found.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 — Contingency Planning Guide

Reading how contingency planning is positioned relative to organisational resilience and to the other planning an organisation already does, rather than as an IT document about systems

Open NIST resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Agree tolerable downtime per service with the business owner, in writing.
  • Define and rehearse a manual mode for the services where downtime is most damaging.
  • Exercise the plan with the people who would run it, including outside working hours.
  • Reconcile the plan against actual supplier commitments at least annually.
  • Treat availability decisions as security decisions, since they are usually the same decision.
